payload.business_story_markdown:
## The main point

XP Inc. is growing its asset base quickly, but it is earning less per unit of that asset base. In 2Q26 (second quarter of 2026), client assets reached R$1.535 trillion, up 12% year on year. Net inflow was R$28 billion, against R$10 billion in 2Q25. Yet the annualized retail take rate fell 5 basis points year on year to 1.20%, the net margin fell to 28.3% from 29.4%, and active clients grew only 1% to about 4.8 million. The company is winning money from existing clients and from market appreciation, not mainly from new clients, and the mix of what those clients buy is shifting toward low-fee products ([2Q26 release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260817593369/en/XP-Inc.-Reports-Second-Quarter-2026-Results)).

That is the central tension. Strong flows and strong capital support the growth story. Falling fee yield and falling margin test it.

## What XP sells and to whom

XP describes itself as a Brazil-focused, technology-enabled financial platform. It sells investment products and financial services through a low-fee model. The retail segment covers equities, fixed income, a funds platform, retirement plans, cards, credit, insurance and other lines. The wholesale bank covers corporate credit, derivatives, foreign exchange and trading, issuer services and institutional clients.

In 2Q26, retail produced R$3,881 million of R$5,056 million gross revenue, and the wholesale bank produced R$1,175 million, up 32% year on year. Total gross revenue grew 8% and net revenue grew 9%. Earnings before tax were R$1,565 million, up 15%, for a 32.0% EBT margin. Diluted EPS was R$2.67.

The revenue model is fee- and spread-based. Retail revenue comes from client assets, transactions and product sales. Wholesale revenue comes from lending spreads, trading and capital-market activity. Distribution runs through 18.4 thousand total advisors, including independent advisors and wealth managers.

Customers are mainly Brazilian retail investors, plus corporate and institutional clients, debt issuers, retirement-plan holders (R$101 billion in client assets), cardholders (1.6 million active cards) and borrowers (R$77.9 billion expanded loan portfolio). The evidence does not split revenue or assets cleanly between mass retail and high-net-worth clients, so revenue quality by wealth tier is an open question.

## What is changing

The demand picture is strong in volume and weaker in price. Total net inflow rose 188% year on year to R$28 billion, and retail net inflow rose 28% to R$20 billion. Over the year, R$103 billion of net inflow and R$60 billion of market appreciation lifted client assets.

But retail fixed-income revenue fell 16% year on year. A third-party summary of the 2Q26 earnings call says about 70% of fixed-income sales were low-margin daily-liquidity products, and that debt-capital-market (DCM) volumes were soft. Fewer new fixed-income offerings, especially tax-exempt instruments, also reduced issuer-services revenue. The same summary reports more than R$400 million of mark-to-market losses in the first half of 2026 and expects DCM volumes to stay soft in 3Q26. This summary is a secondary source, not the full transcript, so treat the mechanism as a reasonable explanation rather than a confirmed one.

Costs add pressure. Headcount reached 8,491, up 13% year on year, while active clients grew 1%. People SG&A rose 9% to R$1,109 million, and salary and taxes rose 23% to R$513 million. Staff and pay are expanding faster than the client count.

## What confirms the story

The 17 August 2026 release supports the picture of a scaled platform with capital strength: client assets up 12%, gross revenue up 8%, EBT up 15%, a 20.3% capital ratio, and growth in the funds platform (+23%), corporate revenue (+117%) and insurance (+23%). The investor-relations page independently shows about R$1.534 trillion in client assets, 18,000+ advisors and R$20.2 billion of last-twelve-month gross revenue. XP also disclosed roughly R$2.5 billion of 2026 capital distribution and cancelled about 11.8 million treasury shares, which fits a company returning surplus capital.

On regulation, a CVM settlement dated 22 July 2026 closed a 2017 administrative case against XP Investimentos and founder Guilherme Benchimol. The reported total payment was R$2.685 million, with no admission of guilt. This removes a legacy overhang, though the source is one news article rather than the CVM record. The wider backdrop is mixed: XP's 2025 Form 20-F risk text flags uncertainty around Brazil's October 2026 elections, and a CVM consultation on fund accounting is pending without a clear link to XP's economics.

## Uncertainties that matter

The most consequential unknown is financing and liquidity capacity. The 20.3% figure is a regulatory capital ratio, not cash. The supplied evidence has no cash balance, debt, maturity schedule or free cash flow, so cash runway cannot be calculated.

Second, competitive pressure from Nubank, BTG Pactual and Itaú is a plausible threat to take rate, but it is not source-backed in this evidence.

Third, governance is a watch item. XP disclosed on 16 October 2026 that Martin Emiliano Escobari Lifchitz resigned from the board, and Rodrigo Kede became an interim director. No reason or operating impact is given.

Fourth, employee evidence is thin: a 4.4 out of 5 Glassdoor rating from 97 reviews, plus one detailed 2023 review that criticised management and work-life balance. That is too old and too narrow to call morale a material risk or asset.

## The most consequential fact: a large guidance raise

On September 29, 2026, Iovance raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $410 million to $420 million, up from $350 million to $370 million. The midpoint rose $55 million, about 15.3%, to $415 million, and the company said the new range implies nearly 60% annual growth ([Benzinga report](https://www.benzinga.com/markets/guidance/26/09/62059046/iovance-biotherapeutics-amtagvi-demand-drives-2026-revenue-guidance-bump-stock-soars)). The raise came after a record second quarter, so it is evidence that demand held rather than a one-quarter beat. This matters more than any single quarter, because the company is not yet profitable and the whole investment case rests on volume growth carrying gross profit past operating expense.

## What the company sells

Iovance is a commercial-stage biotechnology company. It sells two medicines. Amtagvi (lifileucel) is a one-time TIL cell therapy for advanced melanoma. TIL means tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte: immune cells are taken from the patient's tumor, grown in a laboratory, and returned to the patient. Proleukin (aldesleukin) is an interleukin-2 medicine. Revenue comes from product sales, not licensing. The [2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1425205/000110465926018899/iova-20251231x10k.htm) says Amtagvi product revenue began in the second quarter of 2024. Full-year 2025 revenue was $264 million.

In the second quarter of 2026, total revenue was $99.3 million, up 66% from a year earlier and 39% from the first quarter. Amtagvi was about $91 million of that, up roughly 51% quarter over quarter and 68% year over year, and it beat the company's own $79 million to $81 million guidance. Proleukin was about $9 million, down from $11 million on wholesaler inventory timing. Gross margin reached an all-time high of 56%, up from 41% in the first quarter of 2026 ([Q2 2026 release](https://ir.iovance.com/node/15956/pdf)).

The margin line is the part that connects revenue to survival. Research and development expense was about $59 million, the fourth consecutive quarterly reduction. Selling, general and administrative expense was about $39 million and roughly flat. Those two items total about $98 million against gross profit of about $56 million, so the quarter still carried an operating loss. The mechanism to watch is simple: each dollar of added revenue now carries a 56% gross margin, while operating expense is being held down. If that continues, the loss narrows without new financing.

## Who buys, and why center growth is not the only lever

Iovance sells to authorized treatment centers (ATCs) that administer Amtagvi, not to patients directly. At the second quarter of 2026 there were 95 active ATCs, and management targets at least 110 by the end of 2026. About one-third are community oncology sites. About 75% of covered patients have private insurance, and payer policies reach about 250 million lives.

The volume figure is worth reading against the center count. The infusion rate was about 50 patients per month across 95 centers, which is roughly half an infusion per center per month. Reported physician awareness was nearly three times higher than a year earlier. This suggests that much of the growth can come from existing centers treating more patients, not only from adding centers. That interpretation is an inference from two disclosed numbers, not a company statement. If it is right, the 110-center target understates the available demand. If per-center use stays low, the 110-center target will not by itself deliver the raised range.

## What is being confirmed

Several independent events support the same story. FDA granted Fast Track designation for lifileucel in soft tissue sarcoma. Canada and Australia approved Amtagvi, and decisions in the United Kingdom and Switzerland are pending. The pipeline reported a 50% objective response rate in six evaluable sarcoma patients and a 40% confirmed response rate in five evaluable endometrial patients. Lung cancer data (LUN-202) are due in the fourth quarter of 2026. Manufacturing is both a constraint and a claimed advantage: each dose is made from one patient's own cells, and the company says its commercial turnaround is 31 days or less, with the only scaled, centralized commercial TIL process approved by FDA.

## What can break the plan

The largest exposure is concentration. Amtagvi was about 92% of second-quarter revenue, so a slowdown in one product moves the whole company. Reimbursement is the second exposure. Private coverage is strong, but a CMS publication places Amtagvi on the traditional New Technology Add-on Payment pathway, and the opened page did not confirm approval, amount, or effective date ([CMS MEARIS](https://mearis.cms.gov/public/publications/ntap/NTP231012V8Y9J)). Medicare is a large missing payer for a high-cost one-time therapy.

Execution risk is real. Complex patient-specific manufacturing must scale with center growth, and employee reviews point to strain: Indeed showed 1.9 out of 5 from 8 Philadelphia reviews as of March 8, 2026, with culture at 1.0 and management at 1.5, and reviewers cited layoffs ([Indeed reviews](https://www.indeed.com/cmp/Iovance-Biotherapeutics/reviews?fcountry=US&floc=Philadelphia%2C+PA)). These are small, self-selected samples, so they flag morale as a risk rather than measure it.

A short-lived scare is worth separating from real risk. A trading article in early October 2026 said the stock fell 7.99% on “latest regulatory setbacks” but named no FDA action, product, or trial. By October 14, 2026, the stock reached a 52-week high after UBS raised its target, and Barclays had raised its target to $18.00 on October 13. The only specific regulatory negative in the evidence is the December 2023 FDA clinical hold on a lung cancer trial ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/us-fda-places-clinical-hold-iovances-lung-cancer-treatment-trial-2023-12-27/)). That is an old precedent for delay risk, not proof of a new event.
